lines.cap: Wrap wire around an iron nail, connect a battery, and suddenly the nail can pick up paperclips.
Disconnect it, and they clatter to the floor. How can a wire switch magnetism on and off?
The answer links **magnetism**, the invisible push and pull of magnets, with **electricity**, the flow of charge around a circuit.
We'll explore magnets and fields, build an electromagnet, wire up and measure circuits, then finish with static.
A **magnet** attracts magnetic materials, and has two ends called **poles**: a **north pole (N)** and a **south pole (S)**.
The golden rule: **like poles repel**. North pushes north away, and south pushes south away.
**Unlike poles attract**: north and south pull together.
Remember: **L**ikes **R**epel, **O**pposites **A**ttract.
Snap a bar magnet in half, and you don't get a north piece and a south piece.
You get **two smaller magnets**, each with a north and a south pole. You can **never** get a single pole on its own.
Only a few materials are **magnetic**: attracted to magnets, and able to become magnets. The big four are **iron, steel, nickel and cobalt**.
Remember: **I** **S**ee **N**o **C**obwebs. Iron, steel, nickel, cobalt. Steel counts because it's mostly iron.
But **not all metals** are magnetic. **Copper**, **aluminium** and **gold** aren't, and nor are plastic, wood or glass.
So recycling centres can pull **steel** cans out from the **aluminium** ones with a magnet.
A magnet can push or pull without touching. Around it is a **magnetic field**: the region where magnetic materials feel a force.
We draw it with **field lines**. Outside the magnet, they point **from north to south**.
Field lines **never cross**: at each point, the field has only one direction.
Where the lines are **closest together**, the field is **strongest**: at the **poles**.
Sprinkle **iron filings** on paper over a magnet, and each one lines up with the field, revealing its pattern.
But filings only show the field's **shape**, not which way it points.
A small **plotting compass** shows the direction too: its needle's north end points along the field.
Try it at home: put a compass beside a magnet, and mark a dot at each end of its needle.
Move the compass on, line it up with your last dot, mark again, and join the dots. You've traced a **field line**, from N round to S.

chapters.title: The Earth as a giant magnet

lines.cap: A **compass** is just a tiny bar magnet that's free to spin. Left alone, it always settles pointing north–south.
That's because **the Earth behaves like a giant bar magnet**. Its field comes from **molten iron** swirling in its **outer core**.
Now the twist. The compass's **north** pole points to the geographic North, and **unlike poles attract**.
So near the geographic North Pole, the Earth must have a **magnetic south pole**!
For centuries, sailors steered by compass when clouds hid the stars. Hikers and pilots still carry one, in case GPS fails.
Earth's field also **shields** us from harmful particles streaming off the Sun.
And pigeons, sea turtles and some birds sense it, and steer by it like a built-in compass.
Science today: rocks show the Earth's magnetic poles have **swapped** many times. Exactly why is still being researched.
A **permanent magnet**, like a fridge magnet, keeps its magnetism for a long time. **Steel** makes good permanent magnets.
A **temporary** (or **soft**) **magnet**, like **pure iron**, is only magnetic near another magnet, or inside a coil carrying a current. It loses its magnetism easily.
Inside iron and steel are tiny magnetic regions called **domains**. Normally they point every which way, and cancel out.
To **magnetise** steel, stroke it repeatedly **in the same direction** with one pole of a magnet, or put it in a coil carrying a current.
The domains **line up**, all pointing the same way, and the steel becomes a magnet.
To **demagnetise** it, jumble the domains again: **heat** it, **hammer** it, or pull it slowly out of a coil carrying **alternating current**.
Iron's domains line up easily, but jumble just as easily. So iron is bad at staying magnetic, but perfect for a magnet you can **switch off**.
Back to our nail. A current flowing through a wire makes a **magnetic field** around it.
Coil the wire into a **solenoid**, and the fields of all its loops add together.
You get a field like a bar magnet's, with a north pole and a south pole. That's an **electromagnet**.
Its big advantage: you can **switch it on and off**. Stop the current, and the magnetism vanishes.
Reverse the current, and the **poles swap** over.
To make it stronger: more **turns** of wire, more **current**, or an **iron core**, which switches off with the current.
Remember **TIC**: **T**urns, **I**ncrease the current, **C**ore.
But a bigger battery only boosts an **electromagnet**. A **permanent** magnet has no battery at all.
A **scrapyard crane** lifts a car with an electromagnet, then drops it by switching off. A permanent magnet would never let go.
Electromagnets also work **bells**, **loudspeakers**, **motors** and **relays**, which are switches worked by a small current. They even float **maglev trains**.
Try it: coil insulated wire thirty times round an iron nail, and touch the bare ends to a **1.5 V** cell. Count the paperclips it lifts!
Never use the mains, and disconnect between tries, as the wire gets warm.
Now for electricity. **Electric current** is the flow of electric **charge** around a circuit.
It needs two things: a **complete loop**, with no gaps, and a **cell** to push the charge round. Two or more cells make a **battery**.
Think of the cell as a **pump**, pushing charge round the loop.
Open a switch or break a wire, and the current stops **everywhere**, instantly.
Close the switch, and the bulb lights at once. The charges drift slowly, but they fill the wire, so they all start moving together.
**Conductors** let current flow: all **metals**, like copper, gold and aluminium, and **carbon**, as graphite.
**Insulators** don't: **plastic**, **rubber**, **glass**, **wood** and **dry air**.
So wires are **copper** inside **plastic**: the copper carries the current, and the plastic keeps it in, and keeps you safe.
Scientists draw circuits with **circuit symbols**: a universal language that anyone, anywhere can read.
A **cell** is a long thin line and a short thick line. The **long** line is **positive**; the short one is **negative**.
Join two or more, and you have a **battery**.
A **lamp** is a circle with a cross inside, and a **buzzer** is a little dome.
A **switch** is a line that lifts to make a gap, or drops to close it.
A circle with a letter is a meter or a motor: **A** for **ammeter**, **V** for **voltmeter**, **M** for **motor**.
A **rectangle** is a **resistor**. With an arrow through it, it's a **variable resistor**.
With a line through it, it's a **fuse**, which **melts** to break the circuit if the current gets too high.
A **diode** is a triangle pointing at a line. It lets current flow only **one way**.
Add two arrows for light, and it's an **LED**: a **light-emitting diode**.
Draw wires as **straight lines** with neat right-angle corners. A solid **dot** marks a **junction**, where wires join.
So here's a cell, a switch and a lamp, in one complete loop.
Components can be joined in two ways. In a **series** circuit, they're all on **one single loop**, one after another.
The current is the **same everywhere** in the loop. It isn't used up: as much flows back into the battery as flows out.
But the battery's push, its **voltage**, is **shared**. Two identical bulbs get **half** each, and the shares add up to the battery's voltage.
So the more bulbs you add in series, the **dimmer** they all get.
And if one bulb breaks, the gap stops the current, so they **all go out**. Old Christmas lights did this: one dud bulb, and the whole string went dark.
In a **parallel** circuit, components sit on **separate branches**, each with its own path through the battery.
Each branch gets the **full voltage**, so the bulbs are **brighter** than in series, and stay bright even when you add more.
The current **splits** at a junction, and the branch currents **add up** to the total from the battery.
And if one branch breaks, the others **keep working**.
That's why homes are wired in **parallel**: each light and socket gets the full mains voltage, and works on its own.
Remember: **series shares the voltage**, and **parallel splits the current**.
To measure **current**, you need an **ammeter**. It reads in **amps (A)**, and goes **in series**, in the loop, so the current flows through it.
In a series loop, it reads the **same wherever you put it**, since the current is the same all the way round.
In a parallel circuit, the readings on the branches **add up** to the reading by the battery.
To measure **voltage**, also called **potential difference**, you need a **voltmeter**. It reads in **volts (V)**.
Voltage is the **push** the battery gives the charge, or the energy transferred by a component.
A voltmeter goes **in parallel**: **across** a component, on its own little branch beside it.
Across two identical bulbs in series on a **3 V** battery, each voltmeter reads **1.5 V**. Together, that's **3 V**.
Remember: **A**mmeter, **A**lways in a line. **V**oltmeter, **V**erily across.
Almost no current gets through a voltmeter, so one put in series by mistake nearly stops the current.
**Resistance** is how hard it is for current to flow through something.
For the same battery, **more resistance** means a **smaller current**.
It's measured in **ohms**. The symbol is the Greek letter omega, **Ω**.
Even wires have resistance. A **longer** wire has **more**, because the charge has further to push through.
A **thinner** wire has more too, with less room for the charge to flow. So **long, thin** wires resist the most.
A **resistor** adds a fixed resistance, to **limit the current** and protect parts like an **LED**.
A **variable resistor**, or **rheostat**, can be adjusted by sliding a contact.
Slide it to add resistance, and the current falls: a bulb dims, or a motor slows. Slide back, and the current rises.
Variable resistors are used in **dimmer switches** and **volume controls**.

chapters.title: Which way does the current flow?

lines.cap: Which way does current flow round a circuit? There are two answers, and you need both.
**Conventional current**, the direction we draw, flows out of the **positive** terminal, round the circuit, and back to the **negative**: **+ to −**.
But the particles that really move in a wire are **electrons**, and they're **negative**.
They're pushed away from the negative terminal, so **electrons flow from − to +**: the **opposite** way!
Scientists picked the direction of current long before anyone knew about electrons, and it stuck.
It makes no difference to how a circuit works. Just be consistent: in exams, draw current arrows from **+ to −**.
Finally, electricity that **stays put**. **Static electricity** is charge that builds up on an object, instead of flowing.
Rub two **insulators** together, like a balloon on your hair, and **friction** moves tiny negative particles called **electrons** from one to the other.
Whatever **gains** electrons becomes **negative**. Whatever **loses** them is left **positive**. Only the electrons move.
And charges follow the same rule as poles: **like charges repel**, **unlike charges attract**.
That's why your hair stands on end: every strand has the same charge, so they repel.
A charged balloon even attracts things with **no charge**, like bits of paper, or a wall.
It pulls their opposite charges a little closer and pushes like charges away, so the near side is attracted more strongly than the far side is repelled. That's **induction**.
**Earthing** removes charge: a conductor to the ground lets electrons flow away, or in, until the object is neutral.
**Lightning** is a giant static spark between clouds and the ground, heating the air to about five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
Flowing fuel can build up charge, and a spark could ignite it, so fuel tankers are **earthed** before refuelling.
But static is useful in **photocopiers** and **laser printers**: a charged drum attracts **toner** powder onto the page.
And that zap from a door handle? Walking on carpet charges you up, then the charge jumps to the metal.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Likes Repel, Opposites Attract**: for poles, and for charges.
**I See No Cobwebs**: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
**TIC**: more **T**urns, **I**ncrease the current, add an iron **C**ore.
**Ammeter, Always in a line. Voltmeter, Verily across.**
**Series shares the voltage; parallel splits the current.**
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: field lines go from **north to south**, and **never cross**.
Two: the Earth's **magnetic south pole** is near the geographic North.
Three: an electromagnet's magnetism **vanishes** when the current is switched off.
Four: more bulbs in **series** means **dimmer** bulbs, not brighter ones.
Five: measure current in **amps**, and voltage in **volts**. Don't swap them.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
Which magnetic pole of the Earth is near the geographic North?
Its magnetic **south** pole. That's what attracts the north end of a compass.
Give three ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
More **turns**, more **current**, and an **iron core**.
How should a voltmeter be connected to a bulb?
In **parallel**: **across** the bulb.
Two bulbs are in series, and one breaks. What happens to the other?
It **goes out**: the single loop is broken.
A rubbed plastic rod becomes negatively charged. What has it gained?
**Electrons**, from the cloth.
Brilliant work. Now try the Magnetism & Electricity quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
